name: Cement Industry
description: Iran manufactures cement for domestic construction and export markets. Understanding the industry requires distinguishing finished cement from clinker, the intermediate material whose production accounts for much of the manufacturing process's energy use and direct carbon emissions.

seo.title: Iran's Cement Industry: Production, Clinker and Environmental Challenges
seo.description: Explore Iranian cement production, the distinction between cement and clinker, and the evidence needed to assess industrial and environmental performance.

content.heading: A construction material with a separate industrial geography
content.content:
Iran's cement industry serves domestic building activity and export markets. The US Geological Survey identifies Iraq, Kuwait and Afghanistan among destinations for Iranian cement and clinker. These are related products, but their production and trade figures should remain separate: clinker is an intermediate material, while finished cement results from further grinding and blending. [s1](https://www.usgs.gov/centers/national-minerals-information-center/iran) [s2](https://www.iso.org/obp/ui?_escaped_fragment_=iso:std:iso:19694:-3:ed-1:v1:en)

This distinction matters when reading industry announcements. A clinker shipment represents a different processing stage from a cement shipment. Combining their tonnages without specifying the measure can obscure what factories actually manufacture and sell.

content.heading: From raw materials to cement
content.content:
The International Organization for Standardization describes cement manufacture as raw-material and fuel preparation, clinker production through high-temperature processing, and the grinding and blending of clinker with other constituents. Its process inventory includes gypsum, limestone, slag and other materials as possible inputs at the cement-grinding stage; the combination depends on the product. [s2](https://www.iso.org/obp/ui?_escaped_fragment_=iso:std:iso:19694:-3:ed-1:v1:en)

A useful assessment therefore asks where an operation sits in this chain. Kiln production and cement grinding have different inputs and emissions boundaries. An increase in finished cement cannot, by itself, establish an equivalent increase in domestic clinker production.

content.title: The principal cement manufacturing stages
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Raw materials"] -->|"Preparation"| B["Prepared raw material"]
  B -->|"High-temperature processing"| C["Clinker"]
  D["Other cement constituents"] -->|"Blending input"| E["Grinding and blending"]
  C -->|"Intermediate material"| E
  E -->|"Finished product"| F["Cement"]
```
content.summary: Arrows describe material processing. This generic manufacturing sequence does not document the equipment or product mix of any particular Iranian factory.

content.title: Iran: hydraulic cement production, 2020–2024
content.interpretation: Output fell in 2021, recovered through 2023 and declined slightly in 2024. These observations do not establish the causes of the changes.

content.heading: Why energy efficiency is only part of the emissions question
content.content:
Cement's direct carbon emissions have two distinct origins: fuel combustion and the chemical decomposition of carbonate raw materials during calcination. Electricity generation and transport can add emissions outside those direct process boundaries. Improving energy supply therefore addresses only part of the manufacturing footprint. [s2](https://www.iso.org/obp/ui?_escaped_fragment_=iso:std:iso:19694:-3:ed-1:v1:en)

IRENA identifies reducing clinker use and changing energy inputs among approaches to cement decarbonization. These are technological pathways, not evidence that Iranian producers have implemented them at a documented scale. [s3](https://www.irena.org/Decarbonising-hard-to-abate-sectors-with-renewables-Enablers-and-recommendations/Industry-sector/Cement)

The practical conclusion is to read production, trade and environmental performance together, while keeping their definitions separate. National output establishes industrial scale; it does not establish plant efficiency, product quality or environmental compliance.

name: Mineral Industries
description: Iran's mineral industries encompass the extraction and processing of metallic ores and industrial minerals. Their economic significance depends on processing stages, infrastructure and environmental management as well as the quantity of material extracted.

seo.title: Iran's Mineral Industries: Extraction, Processing and Water
seo.description: Understand Iran's mineral production, the distinction between ore and refined products, and documented water-management challenges.

content.heading: Several industries within one label
content.content:
Iran's mineral production includes metallic ores and industrial minerals. The US Geological Survey lists bauxite, copper concentrates, gypsum and feldspar among its outputs. It also identifies the Ministry of Industry, Mine and Trade as the sector's permitting and oversight institution. [s1](https://www.usgs.gov/centers/national-minerals-information-center/iran)

Production statistics distinguish material weight from contained metal and separate mining from refining. These categories should not be added into a single national tonnage: successive processing stages can represent the same material more than once. The accompanying bauxite series is consequently a specific output measure, not a measure of the entire mineral economy.

content.title: Iran: bauxite production, 2020–2024
content.interpretation: Bauxite output declined through 2022 and subsequently recovered. The final observation remains below the first; this series does not measure alumina or aluminum output.

content.heading: A regional example: water and copper processing
content.content:
Sarcheshmeh, in Kerman Province in southeastern Iran, illustrates why a mine must be understood together with its processing and waste facilities. A technical paper presented at Paste 2011 described water scarcity as a central consideration in a proposed expansion of the copper complex. Its authors included representatives of an equipment supplier, an engineering company and the National Iranian Copper Industries Company. Their account is valuable engineering evidence, but it is also a project-participant account. [s2](https://papers.acg.uwa.edu.au/d/1104_22_MacNamara/22_MacNamara.pdf)

The paper explains thickened-tailings disposal: equipment removes water from the fine processing residue before disposal, allowing recovered water to return to industrial use. It discusses the relationship between water recovery, disposal space and expansion design. These are connected engineering decisions rather than independent environmental measures. The paper documents contemporary designs and expectations; it does not establish their performance at the present research cutoff. [s2](https://papers.acg.uwa.edu.au/d/1104_22_MacNamara/22_MacNamara.pdf)

content.heading: What historical environmental studies establish
content.content:
A separate study published in 2010 sampled water around Sarcheshmeh and its tailings-water pond. Its public abstract identifies mine waste dumps as important sources of acid mine drainage and reports that mixing with tailings decant water reduced several dissolved-metal concentrations under the studied conditions. Acid mine drainage is acidic water associated with exposed mine materials; the study concerns a particular site and treatment interaction. [s3](https://doi.org/10.3923/rjes.2010.250.260)

This finding should not become a blanket claim that tailings water is clean or that downstream contamination has been resolved. The inspected abstract does not establish current water quality, long-term treatment reliability or conditions at other Iranian mines. Those questions require dated monitoring evidence and clearly defined sampling locations.

For readers comparing mineral projects, the useful questions therefore extend beyond deposits and output. How is material processed? Where does water come from? How are residues stored and monitored? Historical engineering and environmental studies help frame those questions, while current operational evidence is needed to answer them.

name: Automotive Industry
description: Iran's automotive industry combines vehicle manufacturing, component supply and assembly based on domestic and foreign platforms. Its development has been shaped by the major producers Iran Khodro and SAIPA, changing international partnerships and restrictions affecting access to parts and technology.

seo.title: Iran's Automotive Industry: Manufacturers, Components and Production
seo.description: Explore Iran's car manufacturers, international production links, annual passenger-car output and the distinction between manufacturing and assembly.

content.heading: An industry built around vehicles and their supply chains
content.content:
Iran's automotive industry is best understood as a production network. Iran Khodro and SAIPA are central manufacturers, but their factories depend on component suppliers, engineering capabilities and access to external technology. Historical reporting documents production based on French, Korean and Chinese platforms alongside locally developed vehicles. A national badge therefore does not, on its own, establish where a vehicle was designed or how much of its content was manufactured locally. [s2](https://www.automotivelogistics.media/supply-chain/irans-automotive-industry-left-to-rust/183690)

The field also contains distinct businesses. Passenger cars serve a different market from trucks and buses; components can be manufactured independently of final assembly; motorcycles require separate production statistics. Electric vehicles introduce another distinction between a product being announced, imported, assembled and manufactured. These categories provide the organizing questions for this section's manufacturer and technology pages.

content.heading: International partnerships and interrupted production
content.content:
Industry reporting published in 2019 described a reversal after the opening associated with the 2015 nuclear agreement. Proposed investments by PSA and Renault were followed by renewed sanctions and disruption to supplies of parts and technology. The report also described unfinished vehicles awaiting components and financial pressure on suppliers. These observations concern that historical episode; they should not be read as a current inventory count or a description of every factory. [s2](https://www.automotivelogistics.media/supply-chain/irans-automotive-industry-left-to-rust/183690)

The broader lesson is that final assembly can remain vulnerable even when many components are produced locally. A missing imported item can prevent completion of a vehicle. Conversely, assembling imported kits can sustain measured vehicle output without demonstrating equivalent domestic design capability. Production volume and industrial depth are related questions, but they require different evidence.

content.title: Iran: passenger-car production, 2020–2024
content.interpretation: Passenger-car output increased from 2020 through 2022, then declined in both subsequent observations. The series measures production rather than registrations, sales or domestic value added.

content.heading: How to read the production figures
content.content:
The Japan External Trade Organization, or JETRO, reproduces an annual vehicle-production table attributed to the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers, commonly known as OICA. Its table distinguishes passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, trucks and buses. The chart here uses only the passenger-car column, retaining a consistent product category. [s1](https://www.jetro.go.jp/biz/areareports/2025/12940875b2aa9f23.html)

JETRO separately presents company production and sales reported for Iranian calendar years. Those periods overlap Gregorian years and must not be substituted for the calendar-year national series. Sales are also a different measure from production. The distinction prevents apparent discrepancies from being mistaken for changes in industrial performance. [s1](https://www.jetro.go.jp/biz/areareports/2025/12940875b2aa9f23.html)

content.heading: A dated policy development
content.content:
On October 1, 2026, the US Treasury announced additional automotive-sector sanctions measures and designations covering Iran Khodro, SAIPA, Pars Khodro and other businesses. This announcement establishes the US government's action and stated rationale. Its broader allegations about industry relationships and conduct require independent evidence before being presented as established findings. [s3](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0643)

The announcement is not evidence of a measured subsequent fall in production. Establishing effects would require later output, procurement and company evidence. This distinction is particularly important near an editorial cutoff, when an announced restriction may be documented before its operational consequences can be assessed.

content.heading: What would demonstrate technological progress?
content.content:
JETRO's 2025 overview discusses electric-vehicle adoption and charging infrastructure, indicating that the sector's development extends beyond conventional vehicle assembly. An infrastructure initiative, however, should be assessed separately from actual vehicle production and use. [s1](https://www.jetro.go.jp/biz/areareports/2025/12940875b2aa9f23.html)

For an international reader, the useful test is to follow the evidence through the chain: distinguish a prototype from serial production, a locally assembled model from a locally engineered platform, and a charging announcement from operating infrastructure. Output figures provide an essential starting point. A fuller judgment also needs comparable evidence on reliability, safety, emissions, affordability and supplier capability—areas not established by this draft's production series.
